intro:
French spelling and French sounds don't match the way they do in English. Learning the sounds first makes listening, speaking and the TEF/TCF oral tests much easier.

**Tap anything to hear it.** The 🐢 button plays it slower. Listen, copy it out loud, then listen again.

Each sound shows a **mouth guide** with the lip shape. As a Hindi speaker you already know many of these sounds: माँ, हैं, ग़, श, त, द. We use them as shortcuts.

mouth.name: Smile
mouth.en: Corners of the lips pulled back, as for a photo smile.
mouth.hi: Hothon ko smile ki tarah peeche khinchein.

mouth.name: Small circle
mouth.en: Lips pushed forward into a small tight circle, as if blowing out a candle.
mouth.hi: Hothon ko aage karke chhota gol banao, jaise mombatti bujhate waqt.

mouth.name: Big circle
mouth.en: Lips rounded but loose, mouth more open, as for 'aw' in 'law'.
mouth.hi: Hoth gol rakho par munh zyada khula, jaise 'ऑ' bolte waqt.

mouth.name: Open
mouth.en: Jaw dropped, mouth open, as for 'ah' at the doctor.
mouth.hi: Jabda neeche, munh khula, jaise doctor ke saamne 'aa' bolte hain.

mouth.name: Relaxed
mouth.en: Lips and jaw loose and neutral, barely moving.
mouth.hi: Hoth aur jabda dheele, bilkul aaram se.

mouth.name: Through the nose
mouth.en: Air comes out through the nose as well as the mouth.
mouth.hi: Hawa naak se bhi nikalne do, jaise 'माँ' mein.

sections.title: The alphabet
sections.intro:
French letter names look like English ones, but several sound different. Tap a letter to hear its French name.

Watch out for **E** (euh), **I** (ee), and **G / J**, which are swapped compared with English.

items.name: bé
items.en: close to 'bay', with no 'y' at the end

items.name: euh
items.en: close to 'u' in 'fur' without the r
items.tip: E is named 'euh', not 'ee'. 'Ee' is the letter I.

items.name: gé
items.hiRoman: zhe — close to ज़, par naram, buzz ke saath
items.tip: G is named 'zhé' and J is named 'zhee', the opposite of English. Inside words, g before a, o, u is hard like ग.

items.name: hache
items.tip: H is always silent in words: hôtel = 'otel'.

items.name: ji
items.hiRoman: zhee — close to ज़, par naram, buzz ke saath
items.tip: Not 'jay'. And never Hindi ज: jour is 'zhoor', not 'joor'.

items.name: ka
items.en: close to 'ka', with no puff of air
items.tip: A rare letter, mostly in borrowed words.

items.name: o
items.en: close to 'o' in 'go', but with no 'w' at the end

items.name: pé
items.en: close to 'pay', with no puff of air

items.name: cu
items.en: k + the French u sound; not 'queue'
items.hiRoman: k ke baad French u: 'ki' bolo aur hothon ko gol karo
items.tip: In words, qu is just k: quatre = 'katr'.

items.name: erre
items.hiRoman: er — r gale se, ग़ jaisa halka

items.name: té
items.en: close to 'tay', with no puff of air

items.name: u
items.hiRoman: 'ee' bolo, phir hothon ko 'oo' jaisa gol karo
items.tip: See the vowel u below for the full recipe.

items.name: vé
items.hiRoman: ve — upar ke daant neeche ke hoth par

items.name: double vé
items.tip: A rare letter, mostly in borrowed words.

items.name: ixe
items.tip: Almost no common words start with X. You'll meet it inside words: taxi, and in six, dix where it sounds like s.

items.name: i grec
items.tip: Inside words it sounds like i: stylo = 'stee-lo'.

sections.title: Accents and special letters
sections.intro:
Accents are part of the spelling. Some change the sound, others don't.

- **Change the sound:** é, è, ê, ç, and the two dots (ë, ï), which make you say a vowel separately
- **Spelling or meaning only:** à, â, î, û, ù. For example [[à]] (to) and [[a]] (has) sound the same, and so do [[où]] (where) and [[ou]] (or)
- **ô** is always the closed o of [[eau]]

items.title: e with acute accent (accent aigu)
items.body: **Changes the sound.** Always the closed e: close to 'ay' in 'say', but short, with no 'y' glide at the end. Smile a little.
items.hiRoman: e — close to 'khel' wala e, chhota aur saaf

items.title: e with grave accent (accent grave)
items.body: **Changes the sound.** The open e: close to 'e' in 'bed'. Open your mouth a little more than for é.

items.title: e with circumflex (accent circonflexe)
items.body: **Changes the sound.** Same open e as è, close to 'e' in 'bed'. It often marks an old s: [[forêt]] (forest).

items.title: e with two dots (tréma)
items.body: The two dots mean **say this vowel separately** from the one before it. [[Noël]] is 'no-el', not 'nol'.

items.title: a with grave accent
items.body: **Same sound** as a. It only changes the meaning: [[a]] (has) vs [[à]] (to, at); [[la]] (the) vs [[là]] (there).
items.hiRoman: aa — awaaz same, sirf matlab alag

items.title: a with circumflex
items.body: Some speakers make it a little deeper, but you can say it like a normal a. Mostly a spelling mark.

items.title: i with circumflex
items.body: **Same sound** as i (ee). Spelling only.

items.title: i with two dots (tréma)
items.body: Say the i **separately**: [[maïs]] (corn) is 'ma-ees', but [[mais]] (but) is 'mè'.

items.title: o with circumflex
items.body: Always the **closed o**, the same sound as [[eau]]: close to 'o' in 'go' with no 'w' at the end.

items.title: u with circumflex
items.body: **No change** to the sound. It separates words: [[sur]] (on) vs [[sûr]] (sure). In [[goût]] it sits on the ou.

items.title: u with grave accent
items.body: Found in one word only: [[où]] (where). It sounds exactly like [[ou]] (or).

items.title: c with cedilla (cédille)
items.body: **Changes the sound.** The little tail makes c sound like **s** before a, o, u, where it would otherwise be k.

items.title: o and e joined (e dans l'o)
items.body: Usually the **open eu** sound, as in [[heure]]. No Hindi or English match: say ऐ, then round your lips.
items.hiRoman: 'ai' bolo, phir hothon ko gol karo

items.title: The apostrophe (l', j', c')
items.body: Shows a dropped vowel before another vowel. Say it as **one word**, with no pause: [[l'ami]] = 'la-mi'.
items.hiRoman: ek hi shabd ki tarah bolo, beech mein mat ruko

sections.title: Vowel sounds
sections.intro:
French vowels are **pure**: hold one steady sound. Don't let it slide the way English does in 'go' (go-w) or 'day' (da-y).

Many are close to Hindi vowels: आ, ई, ऊ, ए, ऐ, ओ. Two have no Hindi or English match, **u** and **eu**. For these, follow the mouth recipe.

items.label: a
items.how: Drop your jaw and say a short, bright 'ah'.
items.howHi: Munh khol kar chhota sa 'aa' bolo.
items.trap: Don't use the short Hindi अ of 'kal' (that is 'uh'). French a is always open, like a short आ.

items.label: é
items.en: close to 'ay' in 'say', but short with no 'y' at the end
items.how: Smile slightly and say ए. Hold it steady: don't let it slide into 'ee'.
items.howHi: Halka smile karo aur 'ए' bolo. Awaaz ek jaisi rakho, 'ee' mein mat badlo.
items.trap: English speakers say 'ay-ee'. French é is one pure sound.

items.label: è
items.how: Say é, then drop your jaw a little. The mouth is more open than for é.
items.howHi: Pehle 'ए' bolo, phir jabda thoda neeche karo. 'है' wale 'ऐ' ke kareeb.
items.trap: Don't say 'eye' for ai: lait is 'lè', not 'lie'.

items.label: i
items.how: Smile wide and say a short, tight 'ee'.
items.howHi: Achhe se smile karo aur chhota, tight 'ee' bolo.
items.trap: Never the loose 'i' of 'sit' or Hindi इ in 'dil'. Use ई, just short.

items.label: o (closed)
spellings: o at the end of a word
items.en: close to 'o' in 'go', with no 'w' at the end
items.how: Round your lips into a small circle and say ओ. Keep the lips still until the end.
items.howHi: Hothon ko chhota gol karo aur 'ओ' bolo. Aakhir tak hoth hilao mat.
items.trap: Don't add a 'w': beau is not 'bow-w'.

items.label: o (open)
spellings: o before a spoken consonant (bol, porte, homme)
items.how: Round your lips loosely and open your mouth more than for ओ.
items.howHi: Hoth dheele gol, munh 'ओ' se zyada khula. 'डॉक्टर' ka 'ऑ' socho.
items.trap: Don't use a tight ओ here: in porte and homme the mouth is more open.

items.label: ou
items.how: Push your lips forward into a small tight circle and say ऊ. Your tongue pulls back.
items.howHi: Hothon ko aage karke chhota gol karo aur 'ऊ' bolo, jaise 'phool' mein.
items.trap: Don't confuse it with u: [[tout]] (all) vs [[tu]] (you).

items.label: u
items.en: no English match; not 'oo' and not 'you'
items.hiRoman: koi Hindi akshar nahi — 'ee' + 'oo' wale hoth
items.how: Say 'ee'. Keep your tongue exactly where it is. Now push your lips into a small circle, as for 'oo'.
items.howHi: Pehle 'ee' bolo, jeebh wahin rakho, phir hothon ko 'oo' jaisa gol karo.
items.trap: If it sounds like 'oo', your tongue moved back. Keep it forward, as for 'ee'.

items.label: eu (closed)
spellings: œu (at the end of a word)
items.en: no English match; say 'ay' with rounded lips
items.hiRoman: koi Hindi akshar nahi — 'ए' + gol hoth
items.how: Say é (ए). Keep your tongue still and round your lips into a small circle.
items.howHi: Pehle 'ए' bolo, jeebh wahin rakho, phir hothon ko chhota gol karo.
items.trap: Don't say 'oo': deux is not 'doo' (that would be [[doux]], soft).

items.label: eu (open)
items.en: close to 'u' in 'fur' (without the r), with rounded lips
items.hiRoman: koi Hindi akshar nahi — 'ऐ' + gol hoth
items.how: Say è (ऐ, as in है). Keep your tongue still and round your lips loosely.
items.howHi: Pehle 'ऐ' bolo (jaise 'है'), jeebh wahin rakho, phir hothon ko dheela gol karo.
items.trap: At first you can use one eu for both. The open one just has the jaw a bit lower.

items.label: the light e (e muet)
spellings: e (le, de, je, me, ce, que)
items.hiRoman: close to 'kal' ka chhota 'a', hoth halke gol
items.how: Relax your mouth, round the lips just a little, and say a quick 'uh'. In the middle of words it often disappears: samedi = 'sam-di'.
items.howHi: Munh dheela rakho, hoth thode se gol, aur jaldi se 'uh' bolo. Kabhi kabhi yeh bilkul gayab ho jaata hai: samedi = 'sam-di'.
items.trap: Don't say 'lay' for le. That is [[les]] (the, plural).

items.label: oi
items.hiRoman: wa — close to 'wapas', hoth gol se shuru
items.how: Start with lips in a small circle (w), then open quickly to 'a'.
items.howHi: Hoth gol se shuru karo ('w'), phir jaldi se 'aa' tak kholo.
items.trap: Never 'oy' as in 'boy': moi is 'mwa'.

sections.title: Nasal sounds
sections.intro:
Good news: Hindi has nasal vowels too, as in **माँ, हैं, हों**. French has three main ones.

**The hum test:** say the sound, then pinch your nose. If the sound changes, air is going through your nose: you're doing it right.

**The n or m is not pronounced.** It only tells you the vowel is nasal. Before a vowel, or when the n/m is doubled, the vowel stops being nasal: [[bon]] → [[bonne]], [[un]] → [[une]].

items.label: an / en
items.en: no English match; close to 'ah' said through the nose
items.how: Open your mouth for आ, keep the tongue low and back, and let air flow through your nose, as in माँ. The tongue must not touch the roof of your mouth.
items.howHi: 'आ' ke liye munh kholo aur 'माँ' ki tarah hawa naak se jaane do. Jeebh upar mat lagao.
items.trap: The n is NOT pronounced: [[France]] is not 'Frann-s'. Before a vowel it is not nasal: [[an]] (year) is nasal, [[année]] (year) is 'a-né'.

items.label: on
items.en: no English match; close to 'oh' said through the nose, with round lips
items.how: Round your lips into a small circle as for ओ, and let air flow through your nose, as in क्यों.
items.howHi: Hoth 'ओ' jaise gol karo aur hawa naak se jaane do, jaise 'क्यों' mein.
items.trap: The n is NOT pronounced: [[bon]] is not 'bonn'. But [[bonne]] (good, feminine) has a real n and no nasal: 'bonn'.

items.label: in / ain / un
items.en: no English match; close to 'a' in 'bag' said through the nose
items.how: Smile slightly, open your mouth as for ऐ, and let air flow through your nose, as in हैं.
items.howHi: Halka smile, munh 'ऐ' jaisa, aur hawa naak se, jaise 'हैं' mein.
items.trap: The n is NOT pronounced: vin is not 'veen' or 'vinn'. And [[un]] is nasal, but [[une]] is the French u + a real n. Most speakers in France say un like in. Many in Quebec keep a separate un with rounder lips. Both are understood.

sections.title: Consonants that differ from English
sections.intro:
Most French consonants are easy for a Hindi speaker. Your **त द प क** are closer to French than the English versions are.

These are the ones that work differently from English.

items.label: r
items.en: no English match; a soft gargle at the back of the throat
items.hiRoman: gh — close to 'ग़लत', 'ग़ज़ल' wala ग़, par aur halka
items.how: Keep the tip of your tongue down behind your lower teeth. Lift the back of the tongue toward the back of your mouth and let air rub there softly, as in ग़.
items.howHi: Jeebh ki nok neeche ke daanton ke peeche rakho. Gale ke paas se halka 'ग़' bolo, ragad kam rakho.
items.trap: Don't roll the tongue tip like Hindi र, and don't use the English r. Make ग़ softer, not rough.

items.label: j / soft g
items.hiRoman: zh — close to 'ज़', par naram, buzz ke saath
items.how: Say श. Keep the tongue and lips in the same place, and add your voice so the throat buzzes.
items.howHi: 'श' bolo, jeebh aur hoth wahin rakho, aur gale se awaaz (buzz) jodo.
items.trap: Not Hindi ज or English 'j' in 'jam': [[bonjour]] is 'bon-zhoor', not 'bon-joor'.

items.label: ch
items.how: Round your lips a little and say श.
items.howHi: Hoth thode gol karo aur 'श' bolo.
items.trap: Never च: chat is 'sha', not 'cha'.

items.label: gn
items.how: Press the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth and say न्य as one sound.
items.howHi: Jeebh ka beech wala hissa upar lagao aur 'न्य' ek saath bolo.
items.trap: Don't say g + n separately: gagner is 'ga-nyé', not 'gag-ner'.

items.label: ill / il
items.how: The l's disappear and you say a quick y.
items.howHi: 'l' mat bolo, uski jagah chhota sa 'y' bolo.
items.trap: fille is 'fee-y', not 'fill'. A few words keep a real l: [[ville]] (town), [[mille]] (thousand).

items.label: h
items.how: Skip it completely and start with the next letter.
items.howHi: 'h' ko chhod do, seedha agla akshar bolo.
items.trap: A few words with h block linking: les | haricots (no z sound). You'll learn them over time, but the h is still silent.

items.label: th
items.how: Ignore the h and say a plain त.
items.howHi: 'h' ko bhool jao, seedha 'त' bolo.
items.trap: Not थ and not English 'think': thé is 'té'.

items.label: qu
items.how: Say a plain क. The u is silent.
items.howHi: Seedha 'क' bolo, 'u' chup hai.
items.trap: Not 'kw': quatre is 'katr', not 'kwatr'.

items.label: c, g and ç
items.en: before e, i, y: c = 's', g = 's' in 'measure'. Before a, o, u: c = 'k', g = 'g' in 'go'
items.hiRoman: a, o, u se pehle: c = k, g = g. e, i se pehle: c = s, g = zh
items.how: Look at the next letter. e, i or y make c and g soft. ç is always s.
items.howHi: Agla akshar dekho. e, i, y ho to c aur g naram. ç hamesha 's'.
items.trap: To keep g hard before e or i, French adds a silent u: [[guitare]] = 'gi-tar', with a hard g as in ग.

items.label: s between vowels
items.en: one s between two vowels sounds like 'z'; ss is always 's'
items.hiRoman: do vowels ke beech s = z; ss = s
items.how: One s between vowels: buzz it like ज़. Two s: a plain स.
items.howHi: Vowels ke beech ek 's' = 'ज़'. Do 's' = 'स'.
items.trap: [[poisson]] (fish, ss = s) vs [[poison]] (poison, s = z). Be careful in a restaurant!

items.label: t and d
items.en: not English t/d; the tongue tip touches the back of the upper teeth
items.hiRoman: Hindi 'त' aur 'द' jaise, 'ट' aur 'ड' jaise nahi
items.how: Put the tip of your tongue on the back of your upper front teeth, as for त and द. Not further back, as for English t or Hindi ट.
items.howHi: Jeebh ki nok upar ke daanton ke peeche lagao, jaise 'त' aur 'द' mein. 'ट', 'ड' nahi.
items.trap: Many Hindi speakers use ट / ड for English t/d. In French, always use त / द. In Quebec, t and d before i and u sound close to 'ts' and 'dz': [[tu]] ≈ 'tsu', [[dire]] ≈ 'dzir'.

items.label: p, t, k
items.en: no puff of air, unlike English 'pin', 'tin', 'kin'
items.hiRoman: 'प त क' jaise, 'फ थ ख' jaise nahi
items.how: Hold your palm in front of your mouth and say पा. You should feel almost no air. That's French.
items.howHi: Haath munh ke saamne rakho aur 'पा' bolo. Hawa lagbhag mehsoos nahi honi chahiye.
items.trap: Hindi already has both kinds (प vs फ). Pick the plain one: [[pas]] is 'पा', not 'फा'.

items.label: l
items.en: always light and clear, like the first l in 'little'; never the dark 'll' of 'ball'
items.how: Touch the tip of your tongue behind your upper front teeth and keep the back of the tongue low.
items.howHi: Jeebh ki nok upar ke daanton ke peeche, baaki jeebh neeche. Bilkul Hindi 'ल'.
items.trap: At the end of a word (il, sel) English speakers make a heavy 'l'. Keep it light, like ल.

items.label: final consonants
spellings: d, t, s, x, z, p, g at the end
items.hiRoman: aakhri consonant aksar chup rehta hai
items.how: Usually don't say the last consonant: petit = 'peti', grand = 'gran'. But final c, r, f, l are often pronounced: think of the English word **CaReFuL**.
items.howHi: Aakhri consonant aam taur par mat bolo: petit = 'peti'. Par c, r, f, l aksar bolte hain: yaad rakho **CaReFuL**.
items.trap: -er at the end of verbs breaks the CaReFuL rule: [[parler]] is 'parlé', with no r.

sections.title: Silent letters, linking and elision
sections.intro: French writes many letters it doesn't say, and it joins words together. These rules make spoken French sound smooth.

items.title: Silent final letters
items.body:
Most consonants at the end of a word are silent: [[petit]] = 'peti', [[grand]] = 'gran', [[les]] = 'lé'.

Exceptions: final **c, r, f, l** are often pronounced (CaReFuL): [[parc]], [[mer]], [[neuf]], [[sel]].

items.title: Final -e
items.body:
A final e is usually silent: [[table]] = 'tabl'.

But it makes the consonant before it heard: [[petit]] ('pe-ti') vs [[petite]] ('pe-tit', you hear the t), [[grand]] ('gran') vs [[grande]] ('grand', you hear the d). In short words like [[le]], [[je]], [[de]] it is the light e.

items.title: -ent in verbs
items.body:
In verbs with **ils / elles**, the ending -ent is completely silent: [[ils parlent]] sounds exactly like [[il parle]].

In other words -ent is a nasal sound: [[souvent]] (often), [[le vent]] (the wind).

items.title: Liaison (linking)
items.body:
A silent final consonant is spoken when the next word starts with a vowel or silent h. s and x become **z**, t and d become **t**, n stays **n**.

- [[les amis]] = 'lé-za-mi'
- [[vous avez]] = 'vou-za-vé'
- [[un ami]] = 'un-na-mi'

Never after **et** (and): [[et un]] has no t.

items.title: Elision (the apostrophe)
items.body: Short words like **le, la, je, ne, de, que, ce** drop their vowel before a vowel or silent h. The apostrophe shows it. Say it as one word: [[l'ami]] = 'la-mi'.

items.title: Enchaînement (flowing together)
items.body:
A consonant that is already pronounced at the end of a word slides onto the next vowel. [[il a]] sounds like 'i-la', [[elle est]] like 'è-lè'.

French sounds like one long word because of this. Don't pause between words.

sections.title: Numbers
sections.intro: Tap any number to hear it. Pay special attention to 70–99: France and Canada count in twenties there.

groups.note:
- **six, dix:** the x is silent before a consonant ([[six livres]] = 'si livr'), sounds like z before a vowel ([[six amis]] = 'si-za-mi'), and like s at the end ('sis', 'dis')
- **huit:** the t is silent before a consonant ([[huit jours]] = 'ui jour'), but said elsewhere
- **sept:** the p is silent, the t is said: 'sèt'
- 17, 18, 19 are 'ten-seven', 'ten-eight', 'ten-nine'
21 uses **et**: [[vingt et un]]. **vingt** alone is 'vin', but in 21–29 the t is pronounced: 'vint-é-un', 'vint-deux'.
Same pattern as 21–29: **et un** for 31, 41, 51, 61, then a hyphen. In **soixante** the x sounds like s: 'swa-sant'.
70 is 'sixty-ten', 71 is 'sixty and eleven', and so on. Belgium and Switzerland say **septante**, but **Canada and France do not**.

80 is 'four-twenties'. **quatre-vingts** takes an s, but **quatre-vingt-un** does not, and there is no **et** in 81 or 91. In 81–99 the t of vingt is silent: 'katr-vin-un'. 90 is 'four-twenties-ten'. Belgium and Switzerland say **nonante** (and some Swiss say huitante), but **Canada and France do not**.

groups.title: 100 and up
groups.note: **cent:** the t is silent before a consonant and at the end: 'san'. [[cent un]] has no et. **deux cents** takes an s, but not when another number follows: [[deux cent un]]. **mille** never takes an s.

drills.title: u or ou?
drills.explain: For u the tongue stays forward as for 'ee' with round lips. For ou the tongue pulls back, like ऊ.

drills.title: é or è?
drills.explain: é is a closed, smiling ए. è is more open, close to ऐ in है. Honest heads-up: at the end of a word many people in France say both the same way, while Quebec keeps them clearly apart. Make the difference yourself; you'll always be understood.

drills.title: le or les?
drills.explain: le has the light e (a quick 'uh'). les has a clear, smiling é. This is often the only way to hear singular vs plural.

drills.title: an or on?
drills.explain: an is an open आँ through the nose. on has small round lips, like ओं in क्यों.

drills.title: in or an?
drills.explain: in is a smiling ऐं, close to हैं. an is an open आँ, close to माँ.

drills.title: Nasal or not?
drills.explain: In the first word the n is silent and the vowel goes through the nose. In the second, the vowel is normal and you hear a real n.

drills.title: eu or ou?
drills.explain: eu is ए or ऐ said with round lips, tongue forward. ou is a plain ऊ, tongue back.
